title: Viticulture in Burgundy
description: From organic and biodynamic farming to vine age, planting density and harvesting decisions — the viticultural practices that drive Burgundy's exceptional quality.
lessons.0.title: Farming Philosophy: Organic and Biodynamic
lessons.0.slides.0.title: Farming Philosophy: Organic and Biodynamic
lessons.0.slides.0.subtitle: 15 minutes
lessons.0.slides.0.description: Learn why Burgundy has become the global heartland of biodynamic viticulture, and how farming philosophy shapes wine quality and style.
lessons.0.slides.1.title: Three Farming Approaches
lessons.0.slides.1.content: Burgundy's producers span a spectrum: from conventional farming that prioritises yield consistency, through certified organic farming, to biodynamic farming that treats the vineyard as a living system.
lessons.0.slides.1.keyPoints.0: Conventional farming: permits synthetic pesticides, herbicides and fertilisers; prioritises yield predictability
lessons.0.slides.1.keyPoints.1: Organic farming (bio): bans all synthetic treatments; certified by Ecocert or equivalent
lessons.0.slides.1.keyPoints.2: Biodynamic farming (biodynamie): organic + lunar calendar + homeopathic soil preparations (BD 500–508)
lessons.0.slides.1.keyPoints.3: Trend: a growing majority of Burgundy's top estates have adopted organic or biodynamic methods since the 1990s
lessons.0.slides.2.title: 🌿 Biodynamic Farming Principles
lessons.0.slides.2.content: Biodynamic agriculture, developed by Rudolf Steiner in 1924, treats the entire farm as a self-sustaining living organism. In Burgundy it was pioneered by Lalou Bize-Leroy (Domaine Leroy) and Anne-Claude Leflaive (Domaine Leflaive), with legendary results.
lessons.0.slides.2.keyPoints.0: Lunar calendar: work is scheduled around moon phases — root, flower, fruit and leaf days
lessons.0.slides.2.keyPoints.1: Soil preparations: herbal and mineral preparations (BD 500–508) sprayed on vines and soil to stimulate microbial life
lessons.0.slides.2.keyPoints.2: No synthetic chemicals: all interventions must be natural
lessons.0.slides.2.keyPoints.3: Biodiversity: cover crops, hedgerows and mixed plantings support a balanced ecosystem
lessons.0.slides.2.keyPoints.4: Certification: Demeter is the leading biodynamic certification body
lessons.0.slides.3.title: 🌱 Why Organic and Biodynamic Matter for Terroir
lessons.0.slides.3.content: The philosophy behind organic and biodynamic farming goes beyond avoiding chemicals — it is about expressing each parcel's specific character more faithfully in the wine.
lessons.0.slides.3.keyPoints.0: Living soils: healthy microbial activity connects vine roots to the mineral substrate, enhancing terroir expression
lessons.0.slides.3.keyPoints.1: Lower yields: natural farming generally reduces vine vigour, concentrating flavour in fewer berries
lessons.0.slides.3.keyPoints.2: Complexity: biodynamic wines are frequently described as having greater textural depth and persistence
lessons.0.slides.3.keyPoints.3: Challenge: more labour-intensive and weather-dependent; risk of crop loss from disease is higher
lessons.0.slides.4.title: Leading Biodynamic Estates in Burgundy
lessons.0.slides.4.points.0: 🍷 Domaine Leroy (Lalou Bize-Leroy) — perhaps the most celebrated biodynamic estate in the world
lessons.0.slides.4.points.1: 🍷 Domaine Leflaive — pioneered biodynamic viticulture in Puligny-Montrachet for white wines
lessons.0.slides.4.points.2: 🍷 Domaine de la Romanée-Conti (DRC) — biodynamic since 1997, organic since 1985
lessons.0.slides.4.points.3: 🍷 Domaine Trapet Père et Fils — one of the earliest biodynamic producers in Gevrey-Chambertin
lessons.0.slides.4.points.4: 🍷 Domaine Prieuré Roch — radical natural philosophy, unfiltered and unfined
lessons.0.slides.5.title: 🧠 Knowledge Check
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.0.question: What distinguishes biodynamic farming from simple organic farming?
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.0.options.1: B. Biodynamic adds a lunar calendar and special soil preparations to organic principles
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.0.options.2: C. Biodynamic is a legally protected term under French AOC law
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.0.options.3: D. Biodynamic farming prioritises higher yields
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.0.explanati: Biodynamic farming builds on organic principles (no synthetic chemicals) and adds Rudolf Steiner's 1924 framework: scheduling vineyard work according to the lunar calendar, and using herbal and mineral preparations (BD 500–508) to stimulate soil biology.
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.1.question: Which of the following is NOT one of Burgundy's well-known biodynamic estates?
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.1.explanati: Château Mouton Rothschild is a famous First Growth in Pauillac, Bordeaux — not a biodynamic Burgundy estate. Leroy, Leflaive and DRC are all celebrated Burgundy biodynamic producers.
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.2.question: What is Demeter?
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.2.options.1: B. The leading international biodynamic certification body
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.2.options.3: D. A famous Grand Cru vineyard
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.2.explanati: Demeter is the principal international certification body for biodynamic agriculture, named after the Greek goddess of the harvest. A Demeter certificate on a wine confirms that the entire farming process meets biodynamic standards.
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.3.question: According to biodynamic theory, what are 'fruit days'?
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.3.options.0: A. The days when fruit can be sold at market
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.3.options.1: B. Days associated with flowering plants; wine is said to be most expressive when tasted on these days
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.3.options.2: C. Moon phases said to favour harvesting and tasting wine for its fruit character
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.3.options.3: D. The first days of summer in the lunar calendar
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.3.explanati: Biodynamic farmers divide the lunar calendar into four categories — root, flower, fruit and leaf days. Fruit days (associated with the fire/fruit constellations) are considered the best days for harvesting, tasting and working with aromatic expression of grapes.
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.4.question: Why do organic and biodynamic practices generally produce lower yields?
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.4.options.0: A. AOC rules specifically cap yields for certified estates
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.4.options.1: B. Without synthetic fertilisers and growth promoters, vine vigour is naturally lower — fewer, smaller berries
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.4.options.2: C. Biodynamic vines grow more slowly than conventional vines
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.4.options.3: D. They are planted at lower density
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.4.explanati: Without synthetic fertilisers and growth promoters, vine vigour is naturally lower. This means fewer berries per bunch and smaller bunch size — which typically concentrates flavour and reduces volume, a trade-off that top Burgundy estates willingly accept.
lessons.0.slides.6.title: Summary
lessons.0.slides.6.content: Burgundy is the global heartland of biodynamic viticulture. The estates commanding the highest prices and critical acclaim are predominantly those that farm organically or biodynamically — testament to the philosophy that great wine begins in a living, healthy soil.
lessons.1.title: The Vine: Clones, Age and Planting Density
lessons.1.slides.0.title: The Vine: Clones, Age and Planting Density
lessons.1.slides.0.subtitle: 15 minutes
lessons.1.slides.0.description: Clonal versus massal selection, the significance of old vines, and why Burgundy plants at some of the world's highest densities.
lessons.1.slides.1.title: Clonal vs Massal Selection
lessons.1.slides.1.content: Every new vine planting requires a choice: use clonally propagated cuttings (a single selected genetic individual) or massal selection (cuttings from the estate's own best old vines, preserving genetic diversity).
lessons.1.slides.1.keyPoints.0: Clonal selection: consistent, predictable, disease-resistant — but genetically homogeneous
lessons.1.slides.1.keyPoints.1: Massal selection (sélection massale): higher genetic diversity, often produces greater aromatic complexity
lessons.1.slides.1.keyPoints.2: Top estates increasingly favour massal selection from their finest old vines
lessons.1.slides.1.keyPoints.3: The clonal 'crisis': mass planting of high-yield clones in the 1970s–80s lowered overall quality across Burgundy
lessons.1.slides.2.title: ⏳ Vine Age and Wine Quality
lessons.1.slides.2.content: Vine age is one of Burgundy's most prized quality indicators. As vines age their root systems penetrate deeper into the subsoil, accessing more complex mineral layers, while naturally reducing berry yield — concentrating flavour intensity.
lessons.1.slides.2.keyPoints.0: Young vines (under 10 years): not permitted to carry a village AOC label; fruit used for Bourgogne Régionale
lessons.1.slides.2.keyPoints.1: Mature vines (15–30 years): produce good village and Premier Cru level wines
lessons.1.slides.2.keyPoints.2: Old vines (30–60 years): often labelled 'Vieilles Vignes'; deeper roots, natural yield reduction, concentration
lessons.1.slides.2.keyPoints.3: Very old vines (60+ years): exceptional complexity; some DRC Romanée-Conti vines are over 100 years old
lessons.1.slides.2.keyPoints.4: The paradox: old vines produce far less fruit per vine, but what they produce is immeasurably more valuable
lessons.1.slides.3.title: 🌿 Planting Density: Burgundy's Secret Weapon
lessons.1.slides.3.content: Burgundy plants at 10,000–12,000 vines per hectare — among the world's highest densities. This forces vines to compete intensely for water and nutrients, driving roots deep and producing concentrated, complex fruit.
lessons.1.slides.3.keyPoints.0: Standard Burgundy density: ~10,000 vines/ha (row spacing: approximately 1m × 1m)
lessons.1.slides.3.keyPoints.1: Competition effect: each vine fights for resources, limiting fruit load per individual vine
lessons.1.slides.3.keyPoints.2: Deeper roots: competition drives roots 4–6 m into the limestone bedrock, accessing mineral complexity
lessons.1.slides.3.keyPoints.3: Mechanical harvesting is impossible: rows are too narrow for machines — hand picking is compulsory
lessons.1.slides.3.keyPoints.4: Cost implication: far more labour per hectare — a fundamental reason why Burgundy is expensive
lessons.1.slides.4.title: 💡 Key Take-aways
lessons.1.slides.4.points.0: 🍷 Massal selection from old vines is the gold standard for preserving genetic complexity in Burgundy
lessons.1.slides.4.points.1: 🍷 Vine age directly correlates with flavour concentration — 'Vieilles Vignes' on the label matters
lessons.1.slides.4.points.2: 🍷 Extreme planting density is a fundamental quality driver, not just a tradition
lessons.1.slides.4.points.3: 🍷 High density + hand harvesting + low yield = exceptional quality at high cost
lessons.1.slides.5.title: 🧠 Knowledge Check
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.0.question: What is massal selection (sélection massale)?
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.0.options.0: A. Selecting the largest grape bunches at harvest for a separate cuvée
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.0.options.1: B. Propagating new vines from cuttings taken from the estate's own best old vines, preserving genetic diversity
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.0.options.2: C. Cloning a single perfect vine for complete uniformity
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.0.options.3: D. Selecting grapes by sugar content before fermentation
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.0.explanati: Massal selection involves taking cuttings from many of an estate's own best old vines, preserving genetic diversity within the vineyard. This contrasts with clonal selection, where all new vines descend from a single selected individual. Massal selection is associated with greater aromatic complexity.
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.1.question: What does 'Vieilles Vignes' on a Burgundy label indicate?
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.1.options.0: A. The wine was aged in old barrels
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.1.options.1: B. The wine comes from old vines, generally 30+ years
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.1.options.2: C. A specific appellation or vineyard designation
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.1.options.3: D. An estate-bottled wine (mis en bouteille au domaine)
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.1.explanati: Vieilles Vignes (literally 'old vines') on a Burgundy label indicates the wine comes from older vines. There is no legal minimum age definition in France, but the term generally implies vines at least 30 years old, which typically produce lower yields and more concentrated, complex flavours.
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.2.question: Why does high planting density improve wine quality?
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.2.options.0: A. More vines means more grapes per hectare and therefore higher yield
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.2.options.1: B. Vine competition drives roots deeper and reduces yield per vine, concentrating flavour
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.2.options.2: C. High density reduces the risk of spring frost
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.2.options.3: D. Dense rows prevent weed growth, reducing the need for herbicides
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.2.explanati: At Burgundy's density of 10,000–12,000 vines/ha, each vine competes intensely with its neighbours for water and nutrients. This natural stress forces roots deeper into the mineral subsoil and limits the number of berries per vine — concentration is the result.
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.3.question: Why is mechanical harvesting not used in most of Burgundy?
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.3.options.0: A. French AOC regulations categorically forbid mechanical harvesting in Burgundy
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.3.options.1: B. Mechanical harvesters are too expensive to purchase
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.3.options.2: C. Row spacing of approximately 1m is too narrow for harvesting machines
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.3.options.3: D. Machines damage the soil structure of Grand Cru parcels
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.3.explanati: Burgundy's standard row spacing of ~1m (reflecting 10,000 vines/ha density) is physically too narrow for mechanical harvesting equipment. Hand picking is therefore compulsory — adding significantly to labour costs but also enabling selective picking by bunch ripeness.
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.4.question: At what typical planting density are Burgundy Grand Cru vineyards planted?
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.4.explanati: Burgundy's standard planting density is 10,000–12,000 vines per hectare — among the world's highest. This compares with a New World average of 1,000–3,000 vines/ha. The extreme density forces each vine to compete and is a cornerstone of Burgundy's quality philosophy.
lessons.1.slides.6.title: Summary
lessons.1.slides.6.content: Massal selection, old vine cultivation and extreme planting density are three pillars of Burgundy's viticultural philosophy. Together they explain both why great Burgundy is expensive and why it tastes like nowhere else on Earth.
lessons.2.title: The Annual Cycle: From Pruning to Harvest
lessons.2.slides.0.title: The Annual Cycle: From Pruning to Harvest
lessons.2.slides.0.subtitle: 15 minutes
lessons.2.slides.0.description: A month-by-month guide to the Burgundy vine's annual cycle — the critical events that determine style, yield and ultimately quality.
lessons.2.slides.1.title: ❄️ January–March: Pruning Season
lessons.2.slides.1.content: Winter pruning is the single most important decision a Burgundy vigneron makes. The number of buds left on each vine determines both yield potential and canopy architecture for the entire growing season.
lessons.2.slides.1.keyPoints.0: Guyot pruning system: standard in Burgundy; one or two canes retained per vine
lessons.2.slides.1.keyPoints.1: Grand Cru and Premier Cru AOC rules limit the number of buds per vine to control maximum yield
lessons.2.slides.1.keyPoints.2: Pruning timing: later pruning delays budbreak and reduces spring frost risk
lessons.2.slides.1.keyPoints.3: Skilled pruning considers vine balance, sap flow and the previous season's performance
lessons.2.slides.2.title: 🌸 April–June: Budbreak, Flowering and Fruit Set
lessons.2.slides.2.content: These three months define the vintage's potential size. Spring frost is Burgundy's most feared natural hazard — a single night at -2°C can destroy an entire parcel's harvest.
lessons.2.slides.2.keyPoints.0: Budbreak (débourrement): typically early-to-mid April; tender young shoots are extremely frost-sensitive
lessons.2.slides.2.keyPoints.1: Spring frost protection: pot heaters (bougies), wind machines and water spraying keep temperatures above -2°C
lessons.2.slides.2.keyPoints.2: Flowering (floraison): 6–8 weeks after budbreak; warm, dry, still weather is essential
lessons.2.slides.2.keyPoints.3: Fruit set (nouaison): 10–14 days after flowering; determines the maximum number of berries
lessons.2.slides.2.keyPoints.4: Coulure and millerandage: poor flowering weather causes berry drop or uneven berry size, reducing quantity
lessons.2.slides.3.title: ☀️ July–August: Canopy Work and Véraison
lessons.2.slides.3.content: Summer canopy management shapes the microclimate around each bunch, controlling sun exposure, air circulation and the balance of sugar versus acidity. Véraison — the moment berries change colour — is the critical mid-summer pivot.
lessons.2.slides.3.keyPoints.0: Green harvest (vendange verte): cutting off excess bunches in July to concentrate flavour in those remaining
lessons.2.slides.3.keyPoints.1: Leaf removal (effeuillage): exposing clusters to sun and airflow reduces rot risk and promotes flavour development
lessons.2.slides.3.keyPoints.2: Véraison: Pinot Noir turns from green to red-purple; Chardonnay turns golden-yellow
lessons.2.slides.3.keyPoints.3: The 100-day rule: harvest typically falls approximately 100 days after the midpoint of flowering
lessons.2.slides.4.title: 🍇 September–October: The Harvest Decision
lessons.2.slides.4.content: Deciding when to harvest is the most agonising call of the year. The winemaker balances sugar ripeness, phenolic maturity and acid preservation — all while watching the weather forecast.
lessons.2.slides.4.keyPoints.0: Analytical ripeness: laboratory measurements of potential alcohol (sugar), total acidity and pH
lessons.2.slides.4.keyPoints.1: Phenolic ripeness: tasting seeds and skins for tannin softness and absence of green, astringent flavours
lessons.2.slides.4.keyPoints.2: Rain risk: pre-harvest rain dilutes concentration and encourages botrytis and rot
lessons.2.slides.4.keyPoints.3: Hand harvesting advantage: allows selective picking — only the ripest, healthiest bunches are taken on any given day
lessons.2.slides.5.title: 💡 Key Take-aways
lessons.2.slides.5.points.0: 🍷 Winter pruning determines the season's yield potential — it is the first quality gate
lessons.2.slides.5.points.1: 🍷 Spring frost is Burgundy's greatest natural threat — it has devastated vintages in 2016 and 2021
lessons.2.slides.5.points.2: 🍷 Green harvest (July) is a voluntary sacrifice of volume to achieve quality concentration
lessons.2.slides.5.points.3: 🍷 The harvest decision requires simultaneous mastery of chemistry, sensory evaluation and weather forecasting
lessons.2.slides.6.title: 🧠 Knowledge Check
lessons.2.slides.6.questions.0.question: What is 'véraison'?
lessons.2.slides.6.questions.0.options.0: A. The process of pressing harvested grapes
lessons.2.slides.6.questions.0.options.1: B. The colour change of grape berries marking the beginning of the ripening phase
lessons.2.slides.6.questions.0.options.2: C. The legally mandated harvest date published by French authorities
lessons.2.slides.6.questions.0.options.3: D. The final pressing and bottling of the wine
lessons.2.slides.6.questions.0.explanati: Véraison is the mid-summer turning point when grape berries change colour — Pinot Noir from green to red-purple, Chardonnay from green to golden-yellow. It marks the beginning of the ripening phase, during which sugar accumulates rapidly and acidity begins to fall.
lessons.2.slides.6.questions.1.question: What is 'vendange verte' (green harvest)?
lessons.2.slides.6.questions.1.options.0: A. Harvesting only green, unripe grapes for a fresh, high-acid style
lessons.2.slides.6.questions.1.options.1: B. Removing excess bunches in summer while still green, to concentrate quality in the remaining fruit
lessons.2.slides.6.questions.1.options.2: C. Certified organic harvesting without any chemical treatments
lessons.2.slides.6.questions.1.options.3: D. Harvesting before sunrise to preserve aromatic freshness
lessons.2.slides.6.questions.1.explanati: Vendange verte (literally 'green harvest') is the practice of dropping excess unripe bunches, usually in July. By reducing crop load, the vine concentrates energy into the remaining bunches — resulting in more intense, complex fruit at harvest.
lessons.2.slides.6.questions.2.question: Why is spring frost such a critical hazard in Burgundy?
lessons.2.slides.6.questions.2.options.0: A. Frost permanently destroys the vine's woody structure
lessons.2.slides.6.questions.2.options.1: B. The tender young shoots emerging after budbreak can be killed by a single night below -2°C, wiping out the harvest
lessons.2.slides.6.questions.2.options.2: C. Frost prevents flowering in June
lessons.2.slides.6.questions.2.options.3: D. Frost during harvest causes berries to split and rot
lessons.2.slides.6.questions.2.explanati: Burgundy's continental climate means spring frosts are common in April–May, precisely when delicate young shoots are emerging. A single night at -2°C destroys those shoots on affected parcels, eliminating the entire year's crop. The catastrophic frosts of 2016 and 2021 cut production by 30–50% in many villages.
lessons.2.slides.6.questions.3.question: What does the '100-day rule' refer to in Burgundy?
lessons.2.slides.6.questions.3.options.0: A. Wine must be aged for a minimum of 100 days before release
lessons.2.slides.6.questions.3.options.1: B. The approximate number of days between flowering and harvest
lessons.2.slides.6.questions.3.options.2: C. The legal minimum barrel-aging period for Grand Cru wines
lessons.2.slides.6.questions.3.options.3: D. The number of growing days required for Pinot Noir to reach minimum ripeness
lessons.2.slides.6.questions.3.explanati: As a rule of thumb, harvest falls approximately 100 days after the midpoint of flowering. Since flowering occurs in late June, harvest traditionally falls in late September to early October — though climate change has been pushing this date earlier since the 2000s.
lessons.2.slides.6.questions.4.question: What is the key challenge in deciding the harvest date?
lessons.2.slides.6.questions.4.options.0: A. Negotiating the best price with négociants
lessons.2.slides.6.questions.4.options.1: B. Balancing sugar, acid and phenolic ripeness simultaneously against the incoming weather forecast
lessons.2.slides.6.questions.4.options.2: C. Following the AOC-mandated official harvest date
lessons.2.slides.6.questions.4.options.3: D. Matching the taste preferences of the estate's primary importer
lessons.2.slides.6.questions.4.explanati: The harvest decision requires a three-way balance: analytical ripeness (sugar/acid chemistry), phenolic ripeness (tannin softness, absence of green flavours in seeds and skins) and weather risk. An incoming rain front may force an early pick, while a forecast of fine weather tempts producers to wait for maximum complexity.
lessons.2.slides.7.title: Summary
lessons.2.slides.7.content: The Burgundy vine's annual cycle — from January pruning to September harvest — is a sequence of high-stakes decisions. The constant threat of frost, hail and rain explains both the notorious variability of Burgundy vintages and the extraordinary quality when everything aligns perfectly.
lessons.3.title: Harvesting: Sorting, Selection and the Role of the Hand
lessons.3.slides.0.title: Harvesting: Sorting, Selection and the Role of the Hand
lessons.3.slides.0.subtitle: 10 minutes
lessons.3.slides.0.description: Why Burgundy insists on hand harvesting, and how rigorous sorting separates good Burgundy from truly great Burgundy.
lessons.3.slides.1.title: Hand vs Machine Harvesting
lessons.3.slides.1.content: All top-quality Burgundy is hand-harvested. Extreme planting density makes mechanical harvesting physically impossible on most estates, but the philosophical commitment to selectivity is equally important.
lessons.3.slides.1.keyPoints.0: Physical constraint: row spacing of ~1m is too narrow for mechanical harvesting equipment
lessons.3.slides.1.keyPoints.1: Selective picking: human pickers can identify and reject damaged, diseased or unripe bunches on the spot
lessons.3.slides.1.keyPoints.2: Whole-cluster preservation: hand harvesting delivers intact bunches to the winery — critical for whole-cluster winemaking
lessons.3.slides.1.keyPoints.3: Timing flexibility: picking teams can work parcel by parcel as each reaches its individual optimal ripeness
lessons.3.slides.2.title: 🔬 Sorting: The Final Quality Gate
lessons.3.slides.2.content: Sorting (triage) removes substandard material — damaged berries, leaves, rot, unripe clusters — before fermentation begins. At great estates, sorting is meticulous and may occur multiple times.
lessons.3.slides.2.keyPoints.0: Vineyard sorting: pickers reject obviously damaged or diseased clusters at the vine
lessons.3.slides.2.keyPoints.1: Sorting table (table de tri): a winery conveyor belt where a dedicated team inspects every bunch
lessons.3.slides.2.keyPoints.2: Optical sorting: laser/camera technology removes individual substandard berries after destemming (used at elite estates)
lessons.3.slides.2.keyPoints.3: Double sorting: first as whole clusters, then again after destemming — the gold standard for Grand Cru production
lessons.3.slides.3.title: 📊 Sorting Intensity and Vintage Conditions
lessons.3.slides.3.content: The required intensity of sorting varies dramatically by vintage. Great years require little work; challenging years demand exhausting, expensive sorting to preserve quality.
lessons.3.slides.3.keyPoints.0: Great vintage (e.g. 2015, 2010): 5–10% rejected material; sorting is fast and clean
lessons.3.slides.3.keyPoints.1: Difficult vintage (e.g. 2013, 2007): 20–40%+ rejected; sorting is labour-intensive and costly
lessons.3.slides.3.keyPoints.2: Rot management: separating botrytis-affected from healthy fruit in difficult years is critical for quality
lessons.3.slides.3.keyPoints.3: Winemaker's philosophy: most prefer to eliminate all rot; a few accept tiny amounts for additional complexity
lessons.3.slides.4.title: 💡 Key Take-aways
lessons.3.slides.4.points.0: 🍷 Hand harvesting is compulsory at top Burgundy estates — both practically and philosophically
lessons.3.slides.4.points.1: 🍷 Sorting is the final viticultural decision — what enters the vat determines what ends up in the bottle
lessons.3.slides.4.points.2: 🍷 In difficult vintages, skilled estates can still produce exceptional wine through rigorous sorting
lessons.3.slides.4.points.3: 🍷 Whole-cluster winemaking requires hand picking — another reason the best Burgundy is expensive
lessons.3.slides.5.title: 🧠 Knowledge Check
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.0.question: Why is mechanical harvesting generally not used at top Burgundy estates?
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.0.options.0: A. Mechanical harvesters are too expensive to purchase in France
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.0.options.1: B. Row spacing of ~1m is too narrow for machines, and hand picking allows far greater selective quality control
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.0.options.2: C. French AOC regulations categorically forbid mechanical harvesting in all of Burgundy
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.0.options.3: D. Machines damage the clay-limestone soil structure
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.0.explanati: Burgundy's ~10,000 vines/ha planting density creates rows only ~1m apart — too narrow for harvesting machines. But even where machines could theoretically operate, top estates reject them because hand picking enables selective, bunch-by-bunch quality assessment.
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.1.question: What is a 'table de tri'?
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.1.options.0: A. A wine-tasting table used for vertical tastings
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.1.options.1: B. A sorting conveyor belt at the winery where workers remove substandard fruit before fermentation
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.1.options.2: C. A table used for stacking barrels in the cellar
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.1.options.3: D. A ceremonial table used at the Hospices de Beaune auction
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.1.explanati: The table de tri (sorting table) is a conveyor belt in the winery reception area where a team of workers inspects incoming harvest fruit and removes damaged berries, leaves, unripe clusters and any contaminated material before fermentation begins.
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.2.question: What is 'double sorting' (double triage)?
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.2.options.0: A. Sorting fruit both in the vineyard and at the winery sorting table
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.2.options.1: B. Sorting whole clusters first, then sorting again berry by berry after destemming
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.2.options.2: C. Having two separate teams sort the same batch independently
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.2.options.3: D. Sorting twice per day at different temperatures during hot harvests
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.2.explanati: Double sorting involves removing substandard material at two separate stages: first as whole clusters on arrival, then again as individual berries after destemming. This most rigorous approach is used at elite Grand Cru estates such as DRC and ensures the cleanest possible fermentation.
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.3.question: How does rigorous sorting help in a difficult vintage with significant rot?
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.3.options.0: A. It allows producers to blend in healthy fruit from other regions under the same label
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.3.options.1: B. It removes rotten and botrytis-affected berries before they can contaminate the fermentation with off-flavours
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.3.options.2: C. It reduces the natural sulphur content of the wine
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.3.options.3: D. It makes the finished wine taste sweeter by concentrating residual sugar
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.3.explanati: Rotten or botrytis-contaminated berries release laccase enzymes and mould compounds that destroy wine quality if included in fermentation. Rigorous sorting removes this material before it enters the vat, often rescuing a respectable quality wine from an otherwise devastating vintage.
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.4.question: Why does whole-cluster winemaking require hand harvesting?
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.4.options.0: A. Only hand pickers can legally certify whole-cluster AOC wines
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.4.options.1: B. Mechanical harvesters beat and shake the vines, inevitably breaking and crushing the clusters
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.4.options.2: C. Whole clusters ferment faster, so only morning hand picking is viable
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.4.options.3: D. French AOC rules specify whole-cluster fermentation for Premier Cru and Grand Cru wines
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.4.explanati: Mechanical harvesters work by shaking and beating vine canes to dislodge fruit — inevitably breaking clusters in the process. Only hand harvesting delivers whole, intact bunches to the winery — a prerequisite for the whole-cluster fermentation style used by many of Burgundy's top estates, which relies on intact berry and stem structure.
lessons.3.slides.6.title: Summary
lessons.3.slides.6.content: Hand harvesting and meticulous sorting are non-negotiable at Burgundy's finest estates. They add significant cost and time, but represent the final viticultural decision determining what enters the fermentation vat — and ultimately, what ends up in the bottle.
